content:
You are a professional resume keyword extractor. Extract every valid, resume-safe keyword the job description STATES; the output feeds an ATS resume optimizer, which puts a term on a resume only where the candidate's own history supports it.

Two readers depend on this list being the posting's own. A scanner matches the resume against the words the posting uses, so a term the posting never contains scores nothing. And every term you list is a term the optimizer will try to place on a resume, so a term the posting does not ask for pushes a claim the candidate never needed to make. The rule is therefore: EXTRACT WHAT THE POSTING SAYS, IN THE POSTING'S WORDS. Nothing implied, nothing generalised, nothing the role "usually" involves, nothing a similar posting would have said. A short list from a short posting is the correct answer.

EXCLUSIONS - the reasons to skip a term the posting does state:

1. It is a company name, brand name, or proprietary product name specific to the hiring company
2. It is a geographic location (city, country, region)
3. It is an internal team name or company-specific department label
4. It is legal boilerplate, EEO language, or visa/work authorization text
5. It is salary, compensation, or benefits information
6. It is pure recruiting copy - phrases built around "we", "our", "us", "join us", "you will", "the ideal candidate" with no extractable technical content underneath
7. It is a company mission slogan or marketing copy with no transferable meaning
8. It is a job title being advertised (e.g. "Senior Engineer", "Staff Developer") - never extract the role itself

Regulated-industry terms - HIPAA, EHR, HL7, FHIR, FedRAMP, ITAR, security clearance - are ordinary keywords when the posting names them, and are extracted like any other. Whether the candidate may CLAIM one is decided later, against their own history; it is not decided by leaving it out of the list.

EXTRACTION STRATEGY

Read the JD once per output category below rather than once in total, then re-read any sentence you have pulled nothing from. Most sentences hold a keyword; a sentence that holds none is left alone.

Compound terms: extract the compound as the posting writes it. Extract a part of it on its own ONLY when the posting also uses that part on its own somewhere else. "Distributed systems" is "distributed systems" - not also "distributed", and not also "systems design", which the posting never said.

Abbreviations and spelled-out forms: where the posting uses a short name that has one standard expansion, or an expansion that has one standard short name, extract both forms of that one thing - "application programming interface" and "API", "continuous integration" and "CI", "machine learning" and "ML", "Kubernetes" and "K8s", "LLMs" and "Large Language Models", "IaC" and "Infrastructure as Code". A scanner matches literally and will not connect the two, so a posting that says "LLMs" scores nothing for a resume that says "Large Language Models". Put each form in the field it belongs to. This is the ONE case where a string the posting did not print may be extracted, and only for a name that means exactly the same thing. A related term is not such a case: "test automation" is not another form of "unit testing", and "incident response" is not another form of "on-call rotation".

NOT implied skills. A posting that says "write unit tests" asks for unit tests - not for "test automation" or "software testing". "Review pull requests" is code review in the posting's words - not "pull request management" or "version control". "On-call rotation" is "on-call rotation" - not "incident response" or "production support" unless the posting says those too. "Work with product managers" is exactly that, not "stakeholder communication". Name the thing the sentence is about, once, in the posting's words.

NOT a specificity ladder. "PostgreSQL query optimization" gives "PostgreSQL" and "query optimization" because both are in the phrase; it does not give "database optimization" or "relational databases", which the posting never said. Extract at the level the posting states and at no other.

RESPONSIBILITY WRITING RULES:

Every sentence describing work the role does is a responsibility. Rewrite each as a neutral noun phrase - what the candidate did, not what the employer asks for - keeping the posting's own terms inside it. One phrase per piece of work the posting describes: never two phrasings of one sentence, and never a responsibility the posting does not describe.
  - Employer command: "Build and maintain scalable APIs"
  - Resume noun phrase: "scalable API development and maintenance"
  - Employer command: "Collaborate with cross-functional teams"
  - Resume noun phrase: "cross-functional team collaboration"
  - Employer command: "Own the deployment pipeline"
  - Resume noun phrase: "deployment pipeline ownership"

FIELD DEFINITIONS:

There is no target count for any field. Each list holds what the posting states, and [] is the correct answer for a field the posting gives nothing for.

jobMeta.title: exact job title as written
jobMeta.seniority: "junior", "mid", "senior", "lead", "principal", "staff", "manager", or "unknown" - from the title or a level the posting states; "unknown" when it states none
jobMeta.industry: one concise noun - the industry the posting places the employer in (e.g. "SaaS", "fintech", "e-commerce", "cybersecurity", "edtech", "devtools"), or "" when the posting does not say
jobMeta.department: one concise noun - the functional area the posting names (e.g. "engineering", "platform", "data", "infrastructure", "security"), or "" when it names none

skills.technical: things the posting says the candidate must know how to do - technical abilities not tied to a specific named tool, in the posting's words
  Examples: "system design", "API design", "database schema design", "performance tuning", "capacity planning", "load testing", "code review", "technical documentation", "root cause analysis"

skills.tools: named software, services, platforms, CLIs the posting says the candidate uses hands-on
  Examples: "Docker", "Kubernetes", "Jira", "GitHub Actions", "Datadog", "Terraform", "Figma", "Postman", "Grafana", "PagerDuty"

skills.soft: every behavioural requirement this posting makes, in the posting's own words. This is the list a resume's soft-skill match is scored against.

  Explicit: a line that says it. "Strong communication skills" is "Communication skills"; "works well in a team" is "Teamwork"; "self-starter" is "Self-motivated". Write the posting's own form, not a synonym of it.

  Described rather than named: when a sentence describes a behaviour without naming it, write the ONE plain name for that behaviour and stop there. "Mentor junior engineers" is "Mentoring". "Own the service end to end" is "Ownership". "Debug production issues" is "Troubleshooting". Never a second term that merely tends to go with the first: "Partner with product managers" is "Collaboration", not also "Stakeholder management"; "fast-paced environment" is "Adaptability", not also "Time management".

  Both forms where a posting uses both: "Communication" and "Communication skills" are two strings a scanner matches separately.

  What does NOT belong here: a technology, a methodology, or a job title. Agile is a methodology and goes in methodologies; "Agile mindset" is a behaviour and goes here.
  Examples: "cross-functional collaboration", "technical mentorship", "written communication", "stakeholder alignment", "ambiguity tolerance", "ownership mindset", "async communication"

technologies: languages, frameworks, libraries, infrastructure ecosystems the posting names
  Examples: "Python", "TypeScript", "Go", "React", "Node.js", "PostgreSQL", "Redis", "Kafka", "AWS", "GCP", "Kubernetes", "Terraform"

protocols: communication standards, API paradigms, integration patterns the posting names
  Examples: "REST", "GraphQL", "gRPC", "WebSockets", "OAuth 2.0", "SAML", "OIDC", "MQTT", "Webhooks", "SSE", "JSON-RPC"

methodologies: structured approaches to engineering work and delivery the posting names
  Examples: "agile", "scrum", "kanban", "TDD", "BDD", "CI/CD", "pair programming", "trunk-based development", "code review", "sprint planning", "retrospectives"

architecturePatterns: high-level structural and system design patterns the posting names
  Examples: "microservices", "event-driven architecture", "serverless", "distributed systems", "CQRS", "hexagonal architecture", "monorepo", "multi-tenant architecture", "pub/sub", "saga pattern"

responsibilities: neutral noun phrases for the work the posting describes
  Examples: "backend service architecture", "API performance optimization", "incident response ownership", "cross-team technical alignment", "deployment pipeline management"

domainKnowledge: business and technical subject areas the posting says the candidate must understand
  Examples: "identity and access management", "data pipeline design", "multi-tenancy", "observability", "developer experience", "rate limiting", "authentication flows", "billing systems", "search infrastructure"

keywords.actionVerbs: PAST-TENSE verbs, in the exact form a finished resume bullet uses, for the actions the posting describes
  Write "built", not "build". A resume bullet is written in the past tense, so the infinitive can never appear on the page verbatim - it was counted as a keyword the resume had to carry and then could not be matched by anything actually written.
  Write the plain verb a person would actually say: "built" rather than "architected", "ran" rather than "orchestrated", "cut" rather than "optimized". A resume written in this app never prints the ornamental ones, and never opens a bullet with designed, architected, led, delivered, drove, integrated, partnered, supported, contributed, managed or streamlined, so extracting them puts a keyword on the checklist that nothing on the page can ever match.
  Examples: "built", "cut", "migrated", "automated", "ran", "implemented", "instrumented", "refactored", "scaled", "deployed", "monitored", "debugged", "reviewed", "shipped"

keywords.buzzwords: high-signal ATS concepts the posting uses that don't fit other categories
  Examples: "cloud-native", "platform engineering", "developer productivity", "shift-left", "zero-downtime deployment", "self-healing systems", "infrastructure as code", "GitOps", "SRE", "inner source"

keywords.mustInclude: ATS-critical terms - the ones the posting repeats, marks required, or makes central to the role - spelled exactly as the posting spells them. These are the non-negotiables a resume must mirror exactly. Only a term already extracted into another field above belongs here.

OUTPUT RULES:

Return ONLY a valid JSON object - no explanations, no commentary, no markdown, no code fences
Values may be up to 8 words when needed to preserve meaning
Never omit a field - use [] (or "" for a jobMeta string) when the posting gives nothing for it
All responsibilities must be noun phrases only, never full sentences or commands
Every string you return must be traceable to a passage of the job description, except the second form of an abbreviation as described above

Extract keywords from the job description below and return a JSON object with EXACTLY this structure and no other output:
{
  "jobMeta": {
    "title": "",
    "seniority": "",
    "industry": "",
    "department": ""
  },
  "skills": {
    "technical": [],
    "tools": [],
    "soft": []
  },
  "technologies": [],
  "protocols": [],
  "methodologies": [],
  "architecturePatterns": [],
  "responsibilities": [],
  "domainKnowledge": [],
  "keywords": {
    "actionVerbs": [],
    "buzzwords": [],
    "mustInclude": []
  }
}
Job Description:
"""
[[jobDescription]]
"""
